title: ConvMem: Convolutional Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Sep 2026]
    Title:ConvMem: Convolutional Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities, they often struggle with extremely long contexts due to fixed context limits. To address this, sequential approaches like MemAgent extend the effective context by reading text in segments and iteratively updating a fixed-size memory. However, this sequential paradigm suffers from high latency and requires costly reinforcement learning (RL) training, which can lead to overfitting on specific datasets. To overcome these limitations, we propose ConvMem, a training-free, highly parallelizable framework that reformulates long-context reasoning as a hierarchical convolution. Inspired by CNNs, ConvMem treats an LLM prompted with a specific query as a convolutional kernel. This kernel summarizes text segments hierarchically, shortening the reasoning path from a linear chain into a logarithmic tree. Specifically, ConvMem integrates \textit{Configurable Strides} and \textit{Skip Connections} to ensure robust evidence capture and propagation, while employing \textit{Multi-Kernel Convolution} to decompose complex queries into disentangled semantic channels. This design not only mitigates error accumulation but also enables massive parallelization across both text segments and reasoning threads. Experiments on RULER-HotpotQA and RULER-2WikiMultiHopQA demonstrate that ConvMem outperforms training-free baselines and avoids the risk of overfitting to parametric priors often observed in RL-trained models on out-of-distribution tasks.

report.summary: ConvMem is a training-free, parallel long-context framework that treats an LLM as a convolutional kernel to hierarchically summarize text into logarithmic memory.
report.background: Large language models still struggle with extremely long contexts because of fixed context windows and attention costs. Sequential memory agents like MemAgent extend context by reading text in segments and updating a fixed-size memory, but this approach is slow and depends on expensive reinforcement learning, which can overfit to training data. ConvMem draws on convolutional neural networks to reformulate long-context reasoning as a hierarchical convolution: the LLM becomes a kernel that compresses text at multiple levels, turning a linear reasoning chain into a logarithmic tree. This design aims to reduce latency, improve parallelization, and generalize better to out-of-distribution tasks without additional training.
key_points: ConvMem reframes long-context reasoning as hierarchical convolution, where an LLM prompted with a query acts as a convolutional kernel over text segments. Instead of processing a long document step by step, it summarizes chunks at multiple levels, shortening the reasoning path from a linear chain to a logarithmic tree and reducing sequential latency.

The framework adds configurable strides and skip connections. Strides control how aggressively text is compressed, while skip connections preserve important evidence across layers. Together they help prevent information loss and error accumulation, making the memory more robust when key facts are scattered across a long input.

Multi-kernel convolution decomposes a complex query into disentangled semantic channels. This means different parts of the query can guide separate summarization streams, allowing the model to capture multiple evidence types in parallel and then combine them for the final answer.

ConvMem is training-free and highly parallelizable. Unlike RL-trained memory agents, it does not require costly reinforcement learning or task-specific fine-tuning, so it avoids overfitting to parametric priors and can scale across text segments and reasoning threads more easily.
Experiments on RULER-HotpotQA and RULER-2WikiMultiHopQA show ConvMem outperforms training-free baselines and avoids overfitting risks often seen in RL-trained models on out-of-distribution tasks.
report.impact: ConvMem matters because long-context reasoning is a major bottleneck for deploying LLMs on books, codebases, legal files, and multi-hop enterprise search. If its training-free, parallel approach generalizes, it could lower the cost of long-document QA and reduce reliance on expensive RL pipelines. For developers, it suggests memory can be engineered as a hierarchical convolution rather than a sequential agent, opening doors to simpler deployment and better throughput. For regular users, it could mean faster, more reliable answers over very long inputs. The main caveats are benchmark scope and whether real-world tasks match RULER-style multi-hop evaluation.
report.tools: Follow ConvMem's official code release on arXiv or Hugging Face. Compare it with MemAgent, RULER benchmarks, LongBench, and multi-hop QA datasets like HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA. For serving and parallelism, watch vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and Hugging Face TGI. Also track training-free long-context methods such as hierarchical summarization, retrieval-augmented generation, and streaming memory baselines.
